ai.definition: Metallic glasses are amorphous metals that lack the crystalline structure of traditional metals. They offer superior strength, elasticity, and corrosion resistance compared to conventional materials.
ai.howItWorks: Metallic glass is produced by rapidly cooling molten metal to prevent crystal formation, resulting in a disordered atomic arrangement.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional metals suffer from brittleness, low elasticity, and poor corrosion resistance. Metallic glasses address these limitations while offering enhanced mechanical properties.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves melting a metallic alloy and then rapidly cooling it to form an amorphous structure. This is typically done using techniques like casting or sputtering.
ai.buildProcess: Initial steps include alloy selection, melting, and rapid cooling. Post-processing may involve shaping through methods such as forging or extrusion.
ai.costDrivers: High initial development costs due to specialized equipment for rapid cooling, and the need for precise control over the cooling rate. Production costs can be higher than traditional metals due to the complexity of the manufacturing process.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to see increased adoption in high-strength applications as production processes become more refined and cost-effective.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still evolving, but safety standards for metallic glasses will likely follow those of traditional metals. Certification requirements may vary by application and jurisdiction.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the complexity of manufacturing processes and potential issues with long-term mechanical performance. Environmental risks could arise from the energy-intensive nature of production and disposal challenges if not recycled properly.
ai.profitability: Profitability is dependent on market demand for high-strength materials, which can be significant in aerospace and automotive sectors. However, current costs may limit widespread adoption until further technological advancements reduce expenses.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development could focus on improving manufacturing efficiency, reducing production costs, and expanding the range of alloys to suit a broader spectrum of applications.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Total lifecycle energy requirements are high compared to traditional metals but can be offset by material savings in some applications.

glossary.def: Lacking a regular or orderly structure, as in the case of metallic glasses.
Having a highly ordered and repeating atomic structure, typical of traditional metals.

subsystems.name: Alloy design and feedstock
subsystems.role: sets the mixture of metals that can freeze without crystallising.
parts: high-purity elements (zirconium, titanium, copper, nickel, iron, aluminium and others)

subsystems.name: Melting and quenching plant
subsystems.role: melts the alloy and extracts heat fast enough to freeze it as a glass.
parts: water-cooled copper wheel or copper die

subsystems.name: Composite microstructure
subsystems.role: adds a ductile phase to a brittle glassy matrix.

subsystems.name: Forming and shaping
subsystems.role: turns bar or ribbon stock into near-final parts.

subsystems.name: Finishing
subsystems.role: cuts and polishes a hard but brittle material.

subsystems.name: Characterisation and quality control
subsystems.role: proves the part is truly amorphous and stays that way.
parts: electron microscopy and mechanical test frames

buildSteps.title: Choose a glass-forming composition
buildSteps.detail: The alloy is a multi-element mix chosen so the liquid resists ordering into crystals; models and prior data guide the ratio.

buildSteps.title: Melt the master alloy
buildSteps.detail: High-purity metals are melted together under vacuum or inert gas, often remelted several times to even out the mixture.

buildSteps.title: Freeze it faster than it can crystallise
buildSteps.detail: Melt is squirted onto a spinning copper wheel to make thin ribbon, or cast into a water-cooled copper die for bulk shapes. Thicker parts need alloys that tolerate slower cooling — down to a few kelvin per second in the best cases.

buildSteps.title: Build in a ductile phase
buildSteps.detail: Partly crystallising the melt, or adding fibres or particles, leaves soft crystalline dendrites inside the glassy matrix — the 'composite' that stops cracks running straight through.

buildSteps.title: Shape the part
buildSteps.detail: Parts are die-cast to near-net shape, or heated into the supercooled liquid region where the glass softens and can be pressed like a thermoplastic.

buildSteps.title: Machine and finish
buildSteps.detail: Because the material is very hard but brittle, it is cut with diamond tools and ground, lapped or polished rather than machined conventionally.

buildSteps.title: Verify the glass
buildSteps.detail: X-ray diffraction checks there are no crystal peaks, and calorimetry confirms the glass transition and the temperature at which it would crystallise.

buildSteps.title: Join and assemble
buildSteps.detail: Welding destroys the amorphous structure, so parts are usually bonded with adhesives or diffusion-bonded at controlled temperature.

prerequisites.why: trace oxygen and impurities sharply reduce the ability to form a glass.
the melt must not oxidise before it is quenched.
amorphous ribbon is made this way at industrial scale today.

prerequisites.tech: Alloys with low critical cooling rate
prerequisites.why: only a few compositions can be cast thick enough for structural parts.
bulk glass fails suddenly and without warning, which blocks safety-critical use.
the window between softening and crystallising is narrow and hard to hold.

pathway.milestone: amorphous ribbon wound into transformer cores, plus small cast parts such as watch cases and medical instruments
pathway.unlocks: a proven market for the glassy state, mostly in thin or small forms.

pathway.milestone: tougher glass-matrix composites and additively manufactured bulk glass parts
pathway.unlocks: larger, load-bearing pieces that do not shatter.

pathway.milestone: qualified structural components and wear-resistant claddings in aerospace and automotive use
pathway.unlocks: weight savings where strength-to-weight matters most.

pathway.milestone: reliable joining and recycling routes at industrial scale
pathway.unlocks: metallic glass moving from speciality parts to mainstream engineering material.
